frontier.hypothesis: The ledger's reading of the printf argument list is wrong: the third argument is not an independent read of tbl_11dc[D_800A11D5], but something that shares a subexpression with the fourth - which is the only honest way the edge 'arg3's index load depends on arg4's chain' can exist in C.
frontier.mechanism: The solver names exactly one missing graph edge (add_dep 96 <- 107 on the inline chassis) and it recurs across four independent constraints. arg3's lbu and arg4's sll share no register and no memory as the block is currently written, so no statement move can create it - but a DIFFERENT program in which arg3's index is derived from, or aliases, arg4's chain would have it natively. D_800A11D5 sits inside the region that also holds the D_800A11DC table, and D_800A1494/D_800A1495 are the idx pair. A single struct or a single index expression feeding both the third and fourth arguments is the shape to test.
frontier.next_probe: Re-derive the argument list from the format string and the data model rather than from m2c: dump the bytes at D_800161C8 and D_800A11D0-D_800A11E0 and D_800A1490-D_800A1498, and check whether D_800A11D5 can be reached as a member of the same object the idx pair lives in (or as tbl_11dc's own index byte). Then spell the two candidate forms - (a) arg3's index read through the same pointer local that carries idx_1494, (b) arg3's index and idx0 as two members of one struct - apply each to the INLINE chassis (alt_inline_chassis_13.c, NOT candidate.c), re-run extract.py + solve_inl.py, and check whether constraint k=3 onward becomes baseline-satisfied. Judge by the constraint count the solver reports, never by the sandbox score.

frontier.hypothesis: The same solver loop transfers verbatim to the twins CD_sync and CD_ready, which share this window; one of them may have a chassis where the missing edge is native, and that chassis is then transplantable.
frontier.mechanism: CD_sync lives in the SAME TU (src/system.c), so tmp/sched_solver_work/system.sched.json already contains its blocks; CD_ready's ledger (s36/s46) records a byte-shape-identical do_timeout window and CD_sync s26 records the same {sll,addu,sll} -> jal debug_printf residual. The finding is a property of the shared source idiom, not of CD_datasync's chassis.
frontier.next_probe: With CD_sync's best banked form applied, run the s25 loop for func=CD_sync (blk2.py with the func name changed gives the UID map; the goal comes from asm/funcs/CD_sync.s's own window). Compare which of the fourteen analogous constraints are baseline-satisfied there against CD_datasync's eight. A twin with MORE free constraints has structure CD_datasync's chassis lacks, and that structural difference is the lever.

frontier.hypothesis: Target's block-3 dependence graph is three or more edges from the inline form's, and the missing edges are a property of the ARGUMENT EXPRESSIONS rather than of any spelling of the current ones - so the next rung is a depth-3 add_dep sweep restricted to the arg3 chain, used as an ORACLE to describe the graph, not as a search for a C form.
frontier.mechanism: Depth-2 over all 1332 atoms is exhausted with zero hits, so no two-edge description of target's graph exists. A depth-3 sweep over the full atom set is ~4e8 simulations and is not worth running, but a depth-3 sweep restricted to add_dep atoms whose head or tail is on the arg3 chain (96/99/101/127) is ~1e5 and is affordable.
frontier.next_probe: Restrict enumerate_atoms to add_dep atoms touching UIDs 96,99,101,127 on the inline chassis and run depth 3 against the same 14 constraints. Any hit is a three-edge SPECIFICATION of target's graph, which is then the exact thing the re-derived argument expression must produce; no hit at that restriction promotes the search to the arg2/arg5 chains. Either way the output is a description of the target graph, which is what frontier item 1's data-model re-derivation needs as its acceptance test.
